title: Written on the heart (Jeremiah 31:30–33)
hook: a new covenant: "in their heart will I write it"
carry: a line no exile can carry off

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rachel wept for her children and was told her tears were work that would be rewarded. Your line was there is hope. Did you keep a door open? Today, in the same chapter, a promise about where God's teaching will live. Day eight hundred six.

Torah gets written on a lot of surfaces. On tablets of stone, carried down a mountain. On parchment, rolled into a scroll and lifted in the synagogue. On a tiny scroll tucked into a case on a doorpost, because Deuteronomy says to write these words upon the posts of thy house. Ink, stone, wood. Every one of them can be lost, broken, or left behind when you're carried into exile. In the middle of his chapters of comfort, Jeremiah names one more surface, one that goes wherever you go.
screen: `STONE, PARCHMENT, DOORPOST.` → `ALL CAN BE LEFT BEHIND.` → `ONE MORE SURFACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the promise. "Behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah." Not like the covenant made with their ancestors on the day God took them by the hand out of Egypt, which they broke. And then: "I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people." Look closely at what's written. My law: in Hebrew, torati, my Torah, my teaching. The text doesn't promise a new set of words. It's the same teaching, in a new place. Not outside you, on stone, where you have to go and read it, but inside, where it's simply part of who you are. Deuteronomy already reaches for this: these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart. Proverbs says it too: write them upon the table of thine heart. Jeremiah's twist is who does the writing. In his promise, God writes. And the next verse draws out what that would mean: no one will need to teach a neighbor, saying, know the LORD, "for they shall all know me, from the least of them unto the greatest." Some Jewish readers hear this as the hope of a day when Torah is so deeply learned that it's second nature, the way a language you grew up speaking no longer needs a dictionary. There's a small version of it within reach of anyone: a line learned by heart is a line no exile can carry off.
screen: `A NEW COVENANT.` · then, large: `IN THEIR HEARTS WILL I WRITE IT.` · then: `THE SAME TEACHING, A NEW PLACE.` · `FROM THE LEAST TO THE GREATEST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn one line by heart. Settle, and breathe. Choose one line from these last days on Jeremiah's road: it was never about your size; here, in kitchens and courts and streets; plant a garden there, and pray for the place; there is hope. Or the line from today: I will write it in their hearts. Say it slowly, once, out loud or under your breath. Close your eyes and say it again without looking. Then again, on the out-breath. By the time the bell rings, let it be yours. Tonight, before sleep, see if it's still there. The bell holds the time.
Torati. Hebrew for "my teaching": Jeremiah's promise of a covenant where it is no longer only on stone or parchment, but inside. Today's word.
Your line: a line no exile can carry off. Today, carry your one line without looking it up, and say it once when you need it. Day eight hundred six.

howItsDone: Jews read this promise as part of Jeremiah's chapters of comfort; learning blessings and verses such as the Shema by heart is a familiar part of Jewish education.

Christians also read this passage (it is quoted in the New Testament book of Hebrews); the script deliberately keeps to the Jewish reading and doesn't mention it.
